legacy_conversion_note: Original source (source/Y3/Session 7/LeBron Vs. Michael) includes a full career game-log workbook (LeBron James And Michael Jordan Stats.xlsx) with real, publicly verifiable NBA statistics for both players -- real season-by-season regular-season totals, real season-by-season playoff per-game averages, and real career accolades (championships, MVPs, All-Star selections). No cost/price data needed to be designed for this conversion; every number in Appendix A-D is either a real total from the source workbook or a disclosed, stated derivation from it (see modeling_assumptions). Career shooting percentages and per-game means are computed career-wide (total makes/total attempts, total stat/total games) rather than by averaging each season's own percentage, per Assumption 1/2 -- the standard, correct way career averages are actually reported, and a genuine forcing point for D1-D3. Playoff totals (Appendix B) had to be reconstructed from the source's real per-game-by-season data (multiplied by that season's real games played, summed, rounded) since the workbook only records playoff stats as per-game averages, not season totals -- disclosed as Assumption 4, a close estimate rather than an exact box-score sum. The original case's own 'algorithm' challenge (D5, a self-designed weighted formula) is inherently subjective by design -- this conversion declares career regular-season 3-point percentage as the graded primary metric (a real, close 5.54% gap) precisely because it is one of the case's own required stats (D1) and is close enough to honestly force within SPEC's 20% cap, while leaving the actual GOAT verdict, and dramatic real gaps like assists/game (41% higher for LeBron) or championships (6 vs 4), as disclosed context that feeds each Hero's own algorithm rather than the graded balance test.

modeling_assumptions.text: A career shooting percentage (2-point, 3-point, free-throw) is total career makes divided by total career attempts (Appendix A/B), not the average of each season's own percentage.
A career mean (assists/game, rebounds/game) is total career assists/rebounds divided by total career games played (Appendix A/B), the same reasoning as MA1 applied to counting stats.
Appendix C indexes each season by Career Year (Year 1 = rookie season), not calendar season, so a real mid-career retirement (Jordan's) doesn't misalign the two players' career-length comparison.

Appendix B's playoff totals are reconstructed from the source's real per-game-by-season averages (the only playoff totals the source records), multiplied by that season's real games played and summed, then rounded to the nearest whole make/attempt/assist/rebound -- a close estimate of the true career playoff total, not the exact box-score sum.

The missing-data-element exercise in D2 uses the simple arithmetic mean of LeBron's 18 real season assist totals (sum / 18 = 538.67), not the games-weighted career mean used elsewhere in D2 (7.40 assists/game) -- these are two different, both-real numbers answering two different questions (a season-total average vs. a per-game rate), and the exercise is clearly scoped to the former so it never contradicts the latter.

Every LeBron James statistic in this case (Appendix A, B, C, D) is frozen at the real end of his 18th season, the 2020-21 season, per Appendix E Assumption 5 -- not his stats as of today, since he is still an active player. Jordan's numbers are his real, final, complete career totals.

balance.argument_a: LeBron's real career 3-point percentage (34.49%) is a genuine 5.54% higher than Jordan's (32.68%) -- in an era with far more 3-point attempts league-wide, LeBron's efficiency from deep still edges out Jordan's, and LeBron's real per-game assist (7.40 vs 5.25) and rebound (7.44 vs 6.22) averages are both substantially higher, a real, disclosed gap that speaks to all-around production across a longer career (18 real seasons vs 15).
balance.argument_b: Jordan's real free-throw percentage (83.53%) is a genuine 13.88% higher than LeBron's (73.35%), and Jordan won 6 real championships with 6 real Finals MVPs (a perfect record) against LeBron's 4 and 4 -- Jordan also led the league in scoring 10 real seasons to LeBron's 1. The 3-point gap is real but comes in an era that barely used the 3-point shot the way LeBron's does; Jordan's dominance shows up hardest in the stats that measure winning, not shooting from a distance his own era rarely attempted.
balance.margin_basis: Career regular-season 3-point percentage, computed career-wide from each player's own real total makes and attempts (Appendix A): LeBron's 34.49% is a real 5.54% higher than Jordan's 32.68%. This is one of the case's own required stats (D1), and close enough to honestly force within SPEC's 20% cap -- unlike the dramatic real gaps in assists, rebounds, or championships, which are kept as disclosed context for each Hero's own algorithm (D5) rather than the graded metric.
